Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

An encoder head configured for use with a lithographic exposure tool. The head is devoid of the multiplicity of optical corner-cubes and includes, instead, a single, geometrically substantially perfect cuboid of optically-isotropic material complemented, in operation, with a birefringent lens to form a contraption that, as a unit, splits a single beam of light delivered to the contraption into four measurement (sub-)beams of light (two in xz-plane, two in yz-plane) and causes each of measurement sub-beams to interact with the wafer-stage diffraction grating at the same location twice: upon the first pass by the grating and upon the second pass by the grating. The use of the contraption solves problems of (i) structural complexity of a conventional encoder head for use in an exposure tool, (ii) burdensome alignment of the multitude of optical prisms in the process of forming such encoder head, and (iii) cyclic non-linear errors associated with measurements involving conventional corner-cubes-based encoder heads while, at the same time, reducing the geometrical footprint of the encoder head. The contraption is complemented with a birefringent prismatic element positioned across the axis of the contraption between the cuboid and the birefringent lens.

An encoder head configured for use with a lithographic exposure tool is provided. The head is devoid of the multiplicity of optical corner cubes used in conventional designs and instead includes a single, geometrically substantially perfect cuboid formed from an optically isotropic material. In operation, the cuboid is complemented by a birefringent lens to form an optical contraption that, as a unit, splits a single beam of light delivered thereto into four measurement sub-beams—two in the xz-plane and two in the yz-plane—and causes each measurement sub-beam to interact with the wafer-stage diffraction grating at the same location twice: once during a first pass by the grating and once during a second pass by the grating.

The use of this contraption addresses the problems of: (i) structural complexity associated with conventional encoder heads for exposure tools; (ii) burdensome alignment of multiple optical prisms during formation of such encoder heads; and (iii) cyclic non-linear errors associated with measurements involving conventional corner-cube-based encoder heads. At the same time, the contraption reduces the geometrical footprint of the encoder head. The contraption is further complemented by a birefringent prismatic element positioned across the axis of the contraption between the cuboid and the birefringent lens.

An encoder head is designed for operation in a lithographic exposure apparatus. Rather than using numerous optical corner-cube reflectors, the head employs a single, nearly geometrically ideal cuboid made from optically isotropic material. During use, this cuboid works together with a birefringent lens to create an optical assembly that divides one incoming light beam into four measurement sub-beams: two lying in the xz-plane and two lying in the yz-plane. Each of these measurement sub-beams is directed to interact with the diffraction grating of the wafer stage at the same position two times, once during its first encounter with the grating and again during its second encounter.

This arrangement addresses several drawbacks of conventional encoder heads used in exposure tools, including their structural complexity, the difficult alignment required for multiple optical prisms during assembly, and cyclic nonlinear measurement errors associated with encoder heads based on corner-cube reflectors. At the same time, it decreases the physical size of the encoder head. The optical assembly further includes a birefringent prismatic element arranged transverse to the assembly axis between the cuboid and the birefringent lens.

An encoder head for a lithographic exposure tool can be implemented using a single geometrically precise cuboid made from an optically isotropic material, rather than relying on multiple separate optical corner-cubes. In this arrangement, the cuboid serves as a compact and accurately defined optical body that guides and redirects the measurement beams within the encoder head. By replacing several discrete corner-cube elements with one integrated cuboid, the design simplifies the mechanical and optical architecture of the system.

The cuboid operates in combination with a birefringent lens that splits an incoming light beam into four measurement sub-beams. These sub-beams are directed in two orthogonal measurement planes: two of the sub-beams propagate in the xz-plane, while the other two propagate in the yz-plane. This configuration enables position-related measurements in multiple directions using a single incoming beam and a compact optical arrangement.

During operation, each measurement sub-beam interacts twice with a diffraction grating mounted on the wafer stage. The first interaction occurs during the initial pass of the sub-beam, and the second interaction occurs after the beam has been redirected for a return pass. Importantly, both interactions take place at the same location on the wafer-stage grating. This repeated interaction at a common grating position improves measurement consistency and helps reduce errors associated with spatial variations or imperfections in the grating.

Compared with conventional encoder heads that use multiple corner-cubes, this cuboid-based design offers several advantages. It reduces structural complexity because fewer separate optical components are required. It also lowers the alignment burden, since a single precisely manufactured cuboid is easier to position and maintain than multiple individually aligned corner-cubes. In addition, the common-path-like beam geometry and repeated grating interaction can reduce cyclic non-linear measurement errors. The integrated design also decreases the overall geometrical footprint of the encoder head, making it better suited for compact lithographic systems where space and stability are critical.

A birefringent prismatic element is positioned between the cuboid and the birefringent lens, extending across the axis of the optical contraption. This prismatic element contributes to the beam-conditioning and beam-separation functions of the encoder head, working together with the birefringent lens and the cuboid to establish the desired four-sub-beam measurement geometry. Overall, the arrangement provides a compact, robust, and optically efficient encoder-head architecture for high-precision wafer-stage position measurement in lithographic exposure equipment.

An encoder head for use in lithographic exposure tools can be designed to provide highly accurate wafer-stage position measurement while reducing the number of discrete optical components required in the measurement head. In conventional encoder-head arrangements, several separate optical corner-cubes or retroreflectors may be used to generate multiple measurement beams and return paths. Although such systems can achieve high precision, they also introduce mechanical and optical complexity: each corner-cube must be positioned and aligned accurately, the supporting structure becomes larger and more elaborate, and small optical mismatches can contribute to cyclic nonlinear measurement errors.

The proposed encoder head replaces those multiple corner-cube elements with a single optically isotropic cuboid. This cuboid is used in combination with a birefringent lens and a prismatic optical element to divide one incident input beam into four separate measurement sub-beams. These sub-beams are directed toward selected locations on a wafer-stage grating and are arranged so that each relevant grating location is measured in a double-pass configuration. In other words, the measurement light interacts with the same grating location twice, improving measurement sensitivity and helping to cancel or reduce certain error contributions.

The birefringent lens contributes polarization-dependent beam handling, allowing different polarization components of the input beam to follow controlled optical paths. The prismatic element assists in angularly separating and directing the resulting beams, while the isotropic cuboid provides a compact and stable optical body through which the beams can propagate and be redirected. Together, these components create the required four measurement sub-beams without relying on a set of separately mounted corner-cubes.

By consolidating the optical path into fewer components, the encoder head becomes mechanically simpler and easier to assemble. The reduction in part count also lowers the alignment burden during manufacturing and calibration, since fewer individual reflectors must be positioned with high accuracy. In addition, using a common cuboid for the beam paths can improve optical symmetry and stability, reducing cyclic nonlinearities that may otherwise arise from path differences, component misalignment, or imperfect matching between multiple retroreflectors.

The resulting encoder head has a smaller overall footprint, which is particularly valuable in lithographic exposure systems where space around the wafer stage is limited and where multiple sensors, actuators, and projection-system components must operate in close proximity. A more compact head can be integrated more easily into the machine architecture and may allow improved layout flexibility.

Overall, this design provides a practical and precise optical encoder-head architecture for lithographic positioning systems. By splitting a single input beam into four double-pass measurement sub-beams using an optically isotropic cuboid, a birefringent lens, and a prismatic element, the system achieves accurate grating-based wafer-stage measurement while reducing structural complexity, alignment sensitivity, nonlinear measurement errors, and physical size.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It helps us point to something specific, something already known, or something unique. For example, when we say “a book,” we may mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular one.

This simple word gives sentences clarity and direction. It can make an idea feel more definite, more important, or more connected to the listener. “The sun,” “the world,” “the future,” and “the truth” all sound specific and meaningful because of this tiny word.

Although “the” is easy to overlook, it is essential in everyday speech and writing. It reminds us that even the smallest words can carry great meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense technical summary of an invention involving a compact encoder head for wafer-stage grating measurements in lithography, where a cuboid and birefringent optics cause four beams to double-pass the same grating location.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention concerns a compact optical encoder head for high-accuracy wafer-stage position measurement in a lithographic apparatus, configured to interrogate a diffraction grating mounted on or associated with the wafer stage. The encoder head uses a monolithic or quasi-monolithic cuboid optical body in combination with birefringent beam-splitting and beam-combining optics to generate four measurement beams that impinge on substantially the same local region of the stage grating and each undergo a double pass, thereby improving measurement symmetry, reducing sensitivity to grating non-uniformity, and enabling a small head footprint.

An input radiation beam, typically from a stabilized laser source, is coupled into the cuboid and divided into multiple polarized sub-beams by birefringent optical elements such as Wollaston prisms, Nomarski prisms, Savart plates, beam displacers, or polarization-dependent splitting plates. The cuboid provides accurately defined internal propagation paths, reflection surfaces, and/or interfaces for folding the optical layout. Polarization states are manipulated by retarders, for example quarter-wave or half-wave plates, so that beams are separated, redirected, and recombined with well-defined phase relationships. The arrangement produces four spatially and/or angularly distinct beams that exit the encoder head toward the grating but are arranged to overlap at essentially the same measurement spot on the grating surface.

Each beam is diffracted by the grating, redirected within the head, and returned to the same grating location for a second diffraction interaction. This double-pass geometry causes the measured optical phase to depend strongly on displacement of the grating while common-mode errors from head-to-grating gap variation, local grating pitch variation, surface tilt, and optical path drift are suppressed. By ensuring that all four beams sample the same grating location, the system avoids errors that would otherwise arise if separate beams interrogated different grating regions having local writing errors, contamination, deformation, or thermal expansion differences.

The four double-pass beams are recombined interferometrically to generate one or more phase signals representative of wafer-stage displacement along one or more in-plane degrees of freedom, and optionally out-of-plane displacement, rotation, or yaw depending on the grating orientation and beam geometry. Polarization encoding allows the beams to share much of the same physical aperture while remaining distinguishable until detection. The cuboid block may integrate reflective coatings, partially reflective interfaces, polarizing surfaces, beam-folding mirrors, and alignment references, producing a rigid, thermally stable optical module with reduced component count and reduced alignment burden.

The invention is particularly suited for lithography systems requiring nanometer or sub-nanometer stage metrology in a confined space near the wafer table. The compact encoder head can be mounted adjacent to projection optics or other metrology hardware while maintaining high optical efficiency and measurement robustness. The use of four beams in a symmetric double-pass arrangement enables cancellation of Abbe, tilt, and gap-induced errors, improves immunity to grating imperfections, and supports differential phase processing for high-resolution wafer-stage position feedback during exposure, alignment, or scanning operations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in the style of a patent disclosure, the advantages of replacing a multi-prism corner-cube encoder head in a lithographic exposure apparatus with a cuboid-based optical contraption that creates four measurement beams and reduces footprint, alignment burden, and cyclic nonlinear measurement error.
counterfactuals.output:
In one embodiment, a lithographic exposure apparatus is provided with an encoder measurement system in which a conventional multi-prism corner-cube encoder head is replaced by an optical module comprising a cuboid optical element arranged to generate and direct four measurement beams. The cuboid optical element may comprise a substantially rectangular parallelepiped body having reflective, partially reflective, and/or transmissive surfaces configured such that an incident radiation beam is split, folded, and output as a plurality of spatially separated measurement beams suitable for interaction with one or more encoder gratings or measurement targets.

The use of a cuboid-based optical module provides several advantages over an encoder head employing multiple discrete corner-cube prisms. Because beam generation and beam folding functions are integrated into a single cuboid body, the number of separately mounted optical components is reduced. This reduces the mechanical footprint of the encoder head, permitting the encoder optics to be positioned closer to a substrate table, patterning device table, metrology frame, or other space-constrained portion of the lithographic exposure apparatus. The reduced volume is particularly advantageous in high-throughput lithographic systems, where space near the moving stage is limited and where minimizing mass and envelope size contributes to improved dynamic performance.

The cuboid configuration further reduces alignment burden. In a multi-prism arrangement, each corner cube must be individually positioned and angularly aligned so that the respective measurement beams satisfy predetermined parallelism, spacing, and optical path requirements. By contrast, in the cuboid-based arrangement, the relative positions and angles of the optical interfaces are defined primarily by the geometry of the cuboid and by coatings or internal reflective surfaces formed thereon. As a result, multiple beam paths may be established by a monolithic or quasi-monolithic component. This decreases the number of degrees of freedom requiring adjustment during manufacture, installation, and service, and improves reproducibility between encoder heads.

In addition, the cuboid-based optical module may reduce cyclic nonlinear measurement error. In interferometric or encoder-based position measurement systems, cyclic error can arise from polarization mixing, parasitic reflections, imperfect beam overlap, component misalignment, and differential optical path variations introduced by multiple discrete prisms and interfaces. The integrated cuboid arrangement can provide more stable and symmetric optical paths for the four measurement beams, reduce unwanted relative angular deviations, and limit parasitic beam generation at separate prism boundaries. Consequently, periodic measurement deviations associated with optical non-idealities may be reduced, thereby improving position measurement linearity.

The four measurement beams produced by the cuboid optical element may be used to obtain position information in multiple degrees of freedom, to provide redundancy, or to enable differential measurement of displacement, rotation, or grating position. For example, the beams may be directed toward respective regions of an encoder grating associated with a movable stage, and radiation returning from the grating may be recombined or detected to determine stage position. The geometry of the cuboid may be selected such that the four beams have predetermined spacing and propagation directions while maintaining a compact optical path length within the encoder head.

The disclosed arrangement therefore enables an encoder head having a smaller package size, fewer optical parts, lower assembly complexity, improved beam stability, and reduced cyclic nonlinear error. In a lithographic exposure apparatus, these improvements contribute to more accurate stage-position determination, improved overlay performance, reduced calibration effort, and enhanced manufacturability of the measurement system.

counterfactuals.output:
An encoder head for a lithographic apparatus is disclosed. The encoder head is configured for measuring a position and/or displacement of a wafer stage carrying a diffraction grating. The encoder head comprises a single optically isotropic cuboid, a birefringent prismatic element, and a birefringent lens arranged in a compact optical stack.

In operation, a single input radiation beam is received by the optically isotropic cuboid and directed toward the birefringent prismatic element. The birefringent prismatic element is configured to split the input beam, based on polarization-dependent refraction, into four spatially separated sub-beams. The birefringent lens cooperates with the prismatic element to direct and focus the four sub-beams onto a common measurement region of the wafer-stage diffraction grating.

The optical geometry is selected such that each of the four sub-beams impinges on the same location of the diffraction grating, is diffracted by the grating, and is subsequently redirected so as to interact a second time with that same grating location. After the second interaction, the sub-beams are recombined or routed toward a detector arrangement to generate interferometric measurement signals representative of displacement of the wafer stage.

By using a single optically isotropic cuboid together with birefringent beam-splitting and beam-shaping elements, the encoder head provides a compact and mechanically stable optical assembly. The repeated interaction of each sub-beam with the same grating location reduces sensitivity to local grating imperfections, stage tilt, and alignment errors, while enabling generation of multiple measurement signals from a single input beam. The configuration is particularly suitable for high-precision position measurement in semiconductor lithography systems.
